extracted.intended_audience: infantry officers and NCOs responsible for planning and conducting night operations
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for planning, training, and executing night operations for infantry units, including reconnaissance, deployment, assault and defensive outpost procedures. Emphasises practical techniques, equipment, discipline, and continual practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain orders clearly before quitting assembly
rubrics_metrics.description: Before the position of assembly is quitted the orders are to be clearly explained to all ranks so that everyone may know: (1) the object in view and the direction of the objective; (2) the formation to be adopted at the position of deployment; (3) the part he has to play; (4) his action in case the enemy is not surprised; also that the warnings against firing, talking, striking matches, smoking, etc., are to be repeated two or three times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeat warnings two or three times; ensure every man knows his role and contingency actions; explicitly state formation and direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigid enforcement of prohibitions during training
rubrics_metrics.description: In training a company the prohibitions here alluded to will, of course, be most rigidly enforced at all times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train in peace to form habits for war; carelessness or leniency fosters slackness with serious results on service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose position of deployment relative to force size and enemy alertness
rubrics_metrics.description: The situation of the position of deployment will depend on the strength of the attacking force, and the alertness of the enemy; the smaller the force the nearer to the enemy’s position will this point be fixed. A company can usually get within 300 yards of the enemy’s posts without difficulty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fix deployment point closer if force is small; use 300 yards as a typical guideline for company-level deployments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation at deployment and reserve maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: The Regulations advocate that when the position of deployment is reached the force should be formed in three lines, but with a company it is rarely advisable to have more than two. The front line ... should be in single rank. No more men should be put into the front line than are necessary for the object in view, and the maintenance of a reserve to meet eventualities is of paramount importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider two-line formations at company level, front line single rank; keep a reserve and commander with reserve; avoid committing entire force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use luminous-disc assistants to guide in very dark nights
rubrics_metrics.description: On a very dark night half a dozen assistants, with luminous discs, both on their chests and backs, are provided, and, when the guide has determined on the line, these assistants are placed on it facing towards the guide and covering each other; as the force advances each assistant in turn moves to the far end of the line and covers again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With well-trained assistants expect advance rates of about 0.5–0.75 miles per hour; luminous discs should be handled carefully to avoid detection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a star and pocket electric lamps to find fence passages on starlight nights
rubrics_metrics.description: On a starlight night a star to march on having been chosen, the company is halted, and an officer, with a couple of scouts, each provided with a pocket electric lamp, are sent on to find the best point of passage in the fence; when this point is found an electric light is shown, and the company marches on it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Send scouts with pocket lamps to mark best gaps; intermediate scouts with lights may be posted to maintain direction; handle lamps carefully to minimise front observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: If no stars and fences not parallel, use slow method with guide and assistants
rubrics_metrics.description: If there are no stars, and the fences do not run parallel, the company is halted while the guide moves on to the next fence ... one assistant is posted to mark the spot, while the guide and the others search for the best point of passage ... The company is then brought up to the selected spot, passed through the fence, and again halted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method is slow but accurate; ensure scouts protect the company throughout the operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: If enemy opens fire before assault reach, do not reply and continue advance
rubrics_metrics.description: If, after the position of deployment has been reached, the enemy opens fire, the company must continue its advance until near enough to charge; under no circumstances must the fire be replied to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain momentum toward charging distance; withholding fire avoids giving away range and may preserve surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assault reserve employment and halting supporting lines
rubrics_metrics.description: When the actual assault takes place the second line—and the third line, if there is one—will be halted to await developments; should their assistance be required they will act in prolongation of the first line ... If a force is formed in two lines only the commander must beware of allowing the second line to be drawn into the fight, unless it is absolutely necessary. The retention of some portion of the force intact and ready for instant action is quite as important at night as in the daytime. The commander himself must remain with his reserve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hold back reserves; commit supporting lines only when necessary; commander stays with reserve to react to developments.

rubrics_metrics.name: No pursuit after a successful night assault; immediate reformation and reserve disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Should the assault succeed, no attempt to pursue is to be permitted; the reserve must be at once disposed to meet the counter-attack, and the remainder reformed under its protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise consolidation and counter-attack defence over pursuit; reform under protection of reserve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cheering at the moment of assault: weigh advantages and disadvantages
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the attackers should cheer at the moment of the assault or not is a moot question. For: (1) encourages your own men; (2) discourages the enemy; (3) notifies the assault to neighbouring columns. Against: (1) gives warning to the enemy; (2) gives an indication of the strength of the attacking force. Author favours training men to deliver the assault at night in silence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author prefers silence to avoid alerting enemy supports; train for silent assault to prevent enemy reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough, strict outpost training
rubrics_metrics.description: The first brunt of a night attack necessarily falls on the outposts ... it is, therefore, a matter of supreme importance that the training in outpost duty should be thoroughly carried out ... In carrying out the training of a company in outpost duty the strictest discipline should always be maintained, no irregularity, however trifling, should ever be passed over, and all duties carried out with great care and thoroughness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not neglect outpost duties in manoeuvres; provide realistic, harassing practice under service conditions to build experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconnoitring patrols must supplement groups and piquets
rubrics_metrics.description: The one service which should never be dispensed with is that of the reconnoitring patrols ... the protection afforded by groups and piquets, unless supplemented by a regular system of reconnoitring patrols, is altogether inadequate, and every commander should invariably satisfy himself that the proportion of men told off for patrol duty is sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure adequate numbers for patrol duty; marking piquets/groups with flags is a fallback when manpower is weak but never substitute patrols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Piquet position at night and use of trenches
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless a piquet is protected by obstacles, its best means of defence at night lies in a resolute counter-attack ... a shelter trench affords fair protection in the day time and may be useful at night if the ground immediately in front of it is illuminated by searchlights, but in the dark it loses a great deal of its value ... it is better at night to withdraw the piquets about 30 yards behind the trench; this latter will then form an obstacle likely to break the ranks of an assaulting enemy, and the defenders will have room for the counter-charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not occupy trenches too close to front when unlit; provide clear space for counter-attacks by withdrawing piquets slightly behind parapet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readiness for action of piquets and sentries
rubrics_metrics.description: Piquets must always be ready for action. The men should sleep with their rifles beside them, in the positions they will occupy in the ranks, and must not be allowed to cover their ears when lying down. Either the commander, or the next in command, together with a proportion of the piquet, must always remain awake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange watches so some of piquet are always alert; avoid overreliance on distant groups or single sentry; prevent deep, hard-to-rouse sleep among piquet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide rear cover for forward groups
rubrics_metrics.description: When groups are posted in front of a piquet in open country, they should always have cover in rear to protect them from the fire of their comrades. Groups will remain out with much greater confidence if they feel that they are safe from the fire of their own side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position cover behind forward groups to reduce friendly-fire risk and improve morale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mark routes to and from piquets clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: The route from the support to its piquets, and from the piquets to their groups, should always be clearly marked; scraps of paper, or even green sticks, with the bark peeled off, may be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simple, low-visibility markers to avoid confusion at night; plan and check routes in advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentry challenge protocol to minimise noise
rubrics_metrics.description: The Regulations provide that sentries shall challenge at night, but it is desirable to avoid any noise likely to disclose their position. The signal should be made by the sentry first and replied to by the patrol, but it must be an invariable rule that after the signal has been made one man, and one only, of the patrol shall advance up to the sentry to be recognised. If the signal is not replied to, the sentry will challenge, but in no louder tone than is absolutely necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a prearranged silent/low-noise recognition system; send only one man forward for close recognition; keep voice volume minimal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentries should avoid firing except when necessary and certain
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentries must be taught always to allow persons to approach fairly near to them before challenging, and never to fire, except when it is absolutely necessary to give an alarm, unless they can clearly distinguish the object they fire at and can be fairly certain of hitting it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training reduces frivolous firing; unnecessary shots cause fatigue and annoyance. The French rule (requirement to produce a corpse or blood marks after firing) cited as an excellent deterrent against false alarms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outpost action on warning of night attack: lure, volley, bayonet charge
rubrics_metrics.description: If due warning of the enemy’s advance is received and searchlights are not available, the groups should be withdrawn, and the enemy allowed to approach without any indication that the defenders are aware of his movement ... When he gets within 30 yards, or on dark nights even less, he should be received with one round from every rifle, followed immediately by a bayonet charge. The round should be fired by word of command ... great pains must be taken to impress upon the men the necessity of aiming low.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use controlled volley by command; train men to aim low at night; firing from the hip unproven; simultaneous flank attacks are effective; keep reserves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection criteria for scouts for night work
rubrics_metrics.description: Scouts must be men of good constitution, active, able to bear great fatigue, and to sleep at any hour of the day or night; they must also have acute powers of vision and hearing, be able to make a rough map, to find their way by the compass and the stars, and be absolutely without 'nerves.' They should be thoroughly well acquainted with the appearance of the moon in all its phases ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select scouts for physical stamina, navigational skill, sight/hearing acuity, and steadiness under stress; train their knowledge of moon phases and star movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scout equipment and training standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Each scout should carry a luminous compass and a piece of card, covered with luminous paint, for use under a tracing of the map. If possible, they should be supplied with rubber soles to their boots or, at any rate, the heel pads ... No scout can be considered efficient if he cannot pass through any ordinary outpost line at night whenever he pleases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issue luminous navigation aids and quiet footwear; train scouts to infiltrate through sentry lines at will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scouts to harass enemy outposts and prepare for attack
rubrics_metrics.description: Two or three small parties of well-trained men can keep a whole section of an outpost line in such a state of nervous tension that sleep will be impossible ... In night attacks selected men should be employed to surprise and disable the sentry groups on the line of advance. They should attack the groups from the rear ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ small parties for harassment to induce fatigue; use silent disabling techniques (weighted life preserver or leather bag) to incapacitate sentry with minimal noise and lethality; detail scouts to be ready to throw grenades when attack develops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Searchlight tactics for attackers and defenders
rubrics_metrics.description: When fixed lights are exposed the attackers must endeavour to utilise these dark patches when crossing the zone of light; if travelling beams are used they must lie down before the light reaches them and remain perfectly still till it has passed. In the defence, if searchlights are provided, the officers on outpost duty must endeavour to ascertain what portions of the ground in their front the beams do not light up, and take special measures to watch them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attackers use patches of shadow and stillness to avoid detection; if artillery opens, attackers should continue and assume more open formations; defenders must identify and monitor unlit sectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of flares and improvised torches for lighting piquet approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: When piquets are protected by obstacles an arrangement of flares for lighting the ground in their immediate front is often useful. Empty barrels ... stuffed with straw, rags, or even paper, saturated with paraffin or covered with tar; they should be placed about 50 yards in front of, and a little to the side of, the piquet ... Short sticks, with rags dipped in paraffin, tied round one end, used with effect ... but there is always a risk of the enemy throwing them back again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position flares 50 yards ahead and to the side; have a bold man light at close approach; be aware of the risk of enemy using them or throwing them back.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hand grenades as scout and night-attack weapons
rubrics_metrics.description: These ancient weapons, having been improved, are likely to be largely used in future, and would be specially suitable to issue to scouts ... the sudden explosion of a hand grenade could not fail to have considerable moral effect even if it did little material damage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issue grenades to scouts for close action and to disrupt attacking columns; evidence from manœuvres (crackers) shows notable confusion effect at night.

rubrics_metrics.name: Luminous discs specifications and use
rubrics_metrics.description: Luminous discs are required to mark the directing flank of companies; they should be made of thin board, coated on both sides with luminous paint, and mounted on a pole about 5 feet long. In shape they may be either round or square, but it is useful to have one of a special pattern to mark the directing guide. They may be from 12 inches to 15 inches in diameter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use discs to mark directing guides; have a unique pattern for directing guide for easy identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pocket electric lamps as march points and lamp hooding
rubrics_metrics.description: The pocket lamps used by many officers for reading maps at night answer well as points to march on. They should be provided with a cardboard hood extending about three inches beyond the bulb, to check the lateral spread of the rays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fit lamps with ~3 inch hoods to limit lateral spread; use as discrete march points to guide columns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holding up connecting ropes/tapes to avoid snagging
rubrics_metrics.description: If ropes or tapes (entrenching tapes do well) are used for keeping connection, they must be held up by men placed at intervals of three or four yards. Unless this is done the rope is sure to catch in bushes or stones, and will probably break.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign men to hold rope up every 3–4 yards to prevent catching and breaking; use entrenching tapes as suitable material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passing fences: prefer gateways; make quiet gaps if necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: When possible a gateway will be used for the passage of the troops ... To make a gap in a hedge, choose a weak place, and cut away the wood with saws or knives; axes and billhooks should not be used, as the sound made by them can be heard a long way. Walls of loose stones must be pulled down carefully; wire fences should have a length of wire between two posts cut right out and removed ... Before cutting a taut wire see that it is firmly grasped on both sides ... As sound travels a long way up a wire fence, great care must be taken to avoid jarring the wires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer gateways; avoid noisy tools; when cutting wire, secure both sides to prevent ringing; twist and remove wire ends, and avoid jarring that transmits sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entrenching at night: mark parapet reference points and consider line of sight
rubrics_metrics.description: If trenches which have been dug at night are examined in daylight, it will often be found that owing to the faulty shape of the parapet a good deal of ground close in front of the trench is dead. To obviate this it is advisable to place white objects or electric lamps about 30 yards in front of the trenches, in order that the men, when finishing off the parapet, may so shape it that when firing over it the line of sight will cut the ground at that point. It must also be remembered that in the dark men instinctively fire straight to the front, i.e., at right angles to the parapet, consequently if it is desired to bring fire to bear in an oblique direction some means of marking the required direction are necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark reference points ~30 yards ahead when finishing parapet; plan for oblique fire by marking directions because men naturally fire perpendicular to parapet in the dark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wire entanglements should be irregular and slack
rubrics_metrics.description: In making wire entanglements for the defence of posts any attempt at neatness or regularity is to be avoided; the stakes should be unevenly spaced, and the wire left rather slack with occasional loose loops in it. An entanglement made in this way is harder to pass and to cut than one of the regulation pattern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct irregular, slack entanglements with loose loops rather than neat, regular patterns to increase difficulty of passage and cutting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Night halts: duration management to avoid sleep and delays
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless a halt is to last at least an hour, its duration should not exceed five minutes, otherwise some men will certainly fall asleep, and the operation of waking them causes noise and delay. If a march is to last all night, a halt for a couple of hours, to allow the troops to sleep, is of great benefit, and will diminish but little the total distance covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit short halts to ≤5 minutes to prevent sleep; schedule a multi-hour sleep halt if marching all night to preserve effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of friends at night requires prearranged code signals
rubrics_metrics.description: In repelling a night attack the defenders are always embarrassed by the difficulty of distinguishing between friend and foe, and a previously arranged code of signals is essential if collision between bodies of our own troops are to be prevented. The Russians for this purpose adopted the practice of chanting their National Anthem ... it would be easy to select some simple English song which could not be sung by our enemies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish a recognition code that is simple but not likely to be imitated by enemies; consider using short songs or authentic signals limited to friendly troops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of moon phases and principal stars for navigation
rubrics_metrics.description: An elementary knowledge of the names and positions of the principal constellations and stars is very useful in night work ... The Manual ... states that the lateral movement of a star will not exceed 5° in 20 minutes, and that it is safe to march for about a quarter of an hour on the same star. ... a rough knowledge of [moon] phases enables us to estimate approximately the duration of moonlight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train troops to identify principal stars and moon phases; use star as march point for ~15 minutes; use simple teaching aids (e.g., biscuit demonstration) for moon phases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constant practice across varied conditions is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: The only means of gaining knowledge is to constantly practise Night Operations on all sorts of ground, and in all sorts of weather. ... The accidents that may, and do, happen are so numerous, and the consequences of trivial mistakes so far-reaching, that unless they have been seen they cannot be realised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organise frequent realistic night exercises under varied terrain and weather; supplement theory with repeated practical experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Once committed, act boldly and promptly
rubrics_metrics.description: Although in planning any night operation it is necessary to proceed with the greatest caution, yet, when once the undertaking has been commenced, it must be carried through with the sternest resolution. In the dark the boldest course is generally the best, and every moment of hesitation diminishes the chances of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan cautiously; execute decisively—seize fleeting opportunities, particularly for junior officers seeking distinction.
